newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy and France sidestep EMU at summit start.
newsitem.headline: Italy and France sidestep EMU at summit start.

text.p: France and Italy have kicked off a summit meeting by ignoring a diplomatic spat which flared when French President Jacques Chirac questioned Italy's fitness to found a single European currency.

Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro and Chirac both avoided all reference to European economic and monetary union (EMU) and the lira in banquet speeches on Thursday and extolled the close ties they said bound the two nations.
Earlier, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said the lira would not be on the agenda of the summit in Naples, which he had almost scrapped in anger at Chirac's doubts.
"It is not a dialogue that can be done on a bilateral level," he said.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini later brought the topic to the surface, telling Reuters Financial Television that he expected the lira would return soon to the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), which it crashed out of in September 1992.

"It will not be long before Italy is in the ERM again," Dini said. Asked if that meant by the end of the year, he said: "Soon, but I don't know because this is a matter the treasury ministers are discussing."
Chirac said on Tuesday that Italy might not be able to make the first wave of EMU and blamed the weak level of the lira for hurting French industry.

The remarks infuriated the Italians who are making an all-out effort to qualify for EMU, and triggered a threat to cancel the summit unless Chirac retracted the statements. Chirac rowed back, saying he "ardently hoped" Italy would be among the founders of EMU.

Chirac, toasting his hosts at the banquet, decided not to deliver a prepared statement in which he praised Italian efforts to cut its deficit and added that he hoped Italy would be at France's side at the start of EMU in January 1999.
French officials said the text, which spoke of the "courageous commitment" of Italy to join the vanguard of EMU states, nevertheless reflected Chirac's view.
The French leader told Scalfaro and Prodi that the summit should be an opportunity for the two countries to build on already-close ties to create a closer European Union.
"I hope that we can take another step in the strong ties that exist between Italy and France and that we should put to work for the construction of Europe," Chirac said.
Scalfaro, too, papered over the dispute, likening it to a family argument.
"As always happens between close relations, sometimes there can be some disagreement," he said in his toast.

French and Italian officials said the main topics at the summit would be reform of the European Union's workings, EMU, the Schengen accord on removing border controls, and joint foreign and security policy.
On Wednesday, Chirac's spokeswoman said Italy's ability to be in the vanguard of EMU hinged partly on re-entry to the ERM.

She said France would like to see Italy rejoin the ERM by the end of the year, but at a stronger rate than its current level. Prodi, fearing for the impact of a strong lira on his exporters, is hoping the lira can re-enter at a weaker rate.

Prodi and Chirac will hold nearly two hours of private talks at the 17th century Royal Palace in Naples (from 0745 GMT) before they are joined by financial, foreign, interior, industry, employment and culture ministers.
